source.title: Scaling with Collapse: Efficient and Predictable Training of LLM Families
source.authors: Shane Bergsma; Bin Zhang; Nolan Dey; Shaheer Muhammad; Gurpreet Gosal; Joel Hestness

page_placements.theme: Schedules and normalization enable conditional trajectory prediction

record.file_problem: No major file problem; the full paper is present. Some figure and equation text is flattened in the web extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling-related loss-curve predictability and loss-versus-compute fits using normalized training/validation curves, cross-scale prediction, and alternative training setups, rather than directly reproducing the original scaling-law procedure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own cross-entropy curve, validation-loss scaling, and prediction results. It cites prior work on compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and optimal timescale but does not itself sweep allocations to test the compute-optimal split. The downstream evaluation results measure task accuracy, not pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly about normalized loss-curve collapse, which is not one of the versions. Two of its own results do bear on the claim. Fig. 15 fits validation loss vs. compute as a power law for CompleteP, μP and Celerity families (V1, V7). Fig. 2 and Table 10 show downstream accuracy of Celerity 300M–3.9B rising with compute, with a fitted compute power law (V6). No allocation sweep (V3), no fixed-N shape sweep (V4), no other modality (V5), and no extrapolation of absolute loss from small fits (V2).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right; it should be sharpened. Normalized training-loss curves collapse across sizes (~100M–3.9B) when the LR schedule and TPP are fixed and τ is set optimally for that TPP, so collapse marks compute-efficient training. Deviations from collapse give early diagnostics of problems. A small-scale fitted shape predictor enables early stopping in HP tuning after 10–30% of training. The Celerity family sits on the open-model compute/accuracy frontier.
record.recipe_differences: Studies normalized training and validation loss-curve collapse, optimizer-timescale and TPP controls, and prediction of curve shapes; it does not directly reproduce the original parameter/data/compute final-loss sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Curve shape changes with AdamW timescale τ, TPP, learning-rate schedule, and whether weight decay or τ is held fixed in batch-size sweeps. The reported power-law fit differs between μP and CompleteP. Initial validation-curve alignment varies with warmup proportions; late divergence is reported at 234 TPP.

fits_no_version.finding: A surrogate for normalized training-loss-curve shape, fitted at 111M, predicts normalized curves at 266M–3.3B with MAE 0.54–1.07%, improving with scale. Aligning partial runs to this shape picks the best weight decay after 10–30% of training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalized loss-curve shape is scale-invariant given LR schedule, TPP and τ, and is predictable from small-scale runs.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalized loss curves collapse across 300M–3.9B when TPP and τ are fixed. Collapse is loose with warmup differences, early spikes or high TPP (234). τ and TPP set curve shape.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-curve collapse across model sizes under matched TPP and AdamW timescale.

record.problems: The principal collapse results are largely qualitative and shown in figures without numeric alignment errors. The prediction evaluation reports MAE but no uncertainty estimates. Experiments are limited to the reported model scales and, as the authors note, single-epoch pretraining with AdamW; loss spikes and divergences impair prediction.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported curve values for every model size in the plotted 20-, 80-, and 234-TPP families were extracted; the paper describes these family-level outcomes qualitatively. Figure 14's individual Adam β1/β2 settings and Appendix D.2's additional early-stopping plots were also left out because they do not add a separately quantified result needed for the claim versions represented above.

untested.parts: Separate power laws in parameters and in tokens. Compute fits span only about two orders of magnitude, and no fit-error numbers are given.
Not tested. The paper mentions but does not report extrapolating L(T) from lower-scale power-law fits. Its TLC predictions are of normalized shape only.
Not tested. It assumes the Chinchilla ~20 TPP optimum.
Not tested. There is no depth/width sweep at fixed N.
Not tested. There are no other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer; MoE shape results are a different construct.
Prediction of downstream accuracy from pretraining loss. Held-out quality of the accuracy-vs-compute fit.
Effects of fitting method and parameter counting, and of setup on the compute-optimal split.

missing.what: Fitted compute power laws: Celerity exponent 0.049, μP 0.043, CompleteP 0.051
Downstream accuracy fits in tokens (exp 0.189) and parameters (exp 0.189), plus comparison exponents for Gemma and SmolLM families
Same-size models on SlimPajama vs. the Celerity mix: 300M 45.51 vs. 46.43, 900M 52.02 vs. 54.23

record.verdict_notes: Most extracted rows concern curve-shape collapse, a construct outside every version, so they are relinked to none. The claim-relevant evidence is thin: Fig. 15 compute power laws over about two decades, with no numeric fit error, and Celerity downstream scaling. Fig. 15 exponents are read from the flattened figure text.

versions.untested_parts: Only validation loss versus compute is compared with power-law fits in specific model families; the paper does not test independent power-law scaling in parameters and tokens, nor establish the claimed several-orders-of-magnitude range for all three axes.

Tests normalized TLC prediction from 111M-scale fits at larger scales and early stopping on selected sweeps; it does not directly test whether a conventional power law fitted to small-run final losses predicts much larger runs.
No new sweep of parameter/token allocations at fixed compute or fit of compute-optimal parameter and token counts.
Limited comparisons across the paper's tested architectures, parameterizations, vocabulary, context lengths, and data mixes; it does not map a wide range of depth and width at fixed parameter count.
No tests of other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer. The sparse-MoE experiment is not one of those settings.

Measures downstream benchmark accuracy across Celerity sizes and discusses a compute fit, but does not test prediction of downstream performance from pretraining loss or across a broad range of training regimes.

Shows loss-curve shape and scaling-fit behavior depend on training controls and parameterization, but does not directly compare published exponents or compute-optimal split estimates across fitting methods.
